Part 02 · Understand every option

Q001-Q003 · Reasoning

Q001 · Lesson 1 · foundationReturn to question

What distinguishes demand from a want in marketing?

A. Willingness and ability to buy the preferred solution

A · correct Demand combines a desired solution with willingness and ability to purchase it. Interest alone does not establish that a customer can support a buying decision.

B Awareness may help customers consider alternatives, but it does not show willingness or ability to purchase. Someone can know many solutions without creating demand for any.

C A widely shared preference remains a want unless customers are willing and able to buy. Popularity does not establish the purchasing capacity of that group.

D An underlying requirement describes a need, such as mobility or communication. Demand concerns a preferred solution backed by willingness and ability to make a purchase.

Revisit lesson 1: Marketing begins with a need
Q002 · Lesson 1 · applicationReturn to question

A delivery company promises next-day arrival. A customer receives the parcel after three days, although the contents are excellent. Which interpretation best follows the satisfaction model?

B. Performance fell below an expectation created by the promise

A Product quality contributes to the experience, but it does not automatically cancel a missed delivery expectation. Customers can judge several parts of an offer separately.

B · correct The delivery promise established an expectation that the company failed to meet. This performance gap can create dissatisfaction even when another part of the offer succeeds.

C Demand concerns willingness and ability to buy, not whether delivery later meets expectations. A completed purchase can generate dissatisfaction without changing the meaning of demand.

D Price can influence expectations and perceived value, but satisfaction also reflects performance against promises. The stated delivery commitment is directly relevant to this customer experience.

Revisit lesson 1: Marketing begins with a need
Q003 · Lesson 2 · foundationReturn to question

Which priority most clearly indicates a production orientation?

C. Increasing efficient output and making products widely available

A Persuading customers to buy existing output reflects a selling orientation. Production orientation concentrates more directly on efficient production, scale, affordability and availability of the offer.

B Emphasising advanced features and technical quality reflects product orientation. A production orientation primarily prioritises efficient output and availability rather than maximising the sophistication of features.

C · correct Production orientation emphasises scale, efficient output and availability. These priorities can be appropriate when customers mainly need affordable products and the market faces limited supply.

D Starting with researched customer needs reflects a market-oriented approach. Production orientation starts more directly with the ability to produce efficiently and make the resulting output available.

Revisit lesson 2: Motivation & business orientation
Part 02 · Understand every option

Q004-Q006 · Reasoning

Q004 · Lesson 2 · applicationReturn to question

Interviews show that people join a photography course to improve skills, meet peers and feel proud of their work. How should the marketer interpret these motivations?

D. Recognise that practical and psychological motivations can operate together

A The interviews identify several motivations rather than one universal reason. Reducing every participant to a single category would discard relevant evidence about the course experience.

B Practical learning and social connection can both matter in the same purchase. Evidence of a functional benefit does not eliminate the psychological value customers describe.

C Maslow can support discussion of motivations, but it is not a rigid purchase sequence. The research already shows that several needs influence this decision together.

D · correct The evidence supports overlapping benefits: competence, relationships and achievement. Marketing can address these together while testing their importance for different participants instead of imposing a rigid hierarchy.

Revisit lesson 2: Motivation & business orientation
Q005 · Lesson 3 · foundationReturn to question

What best describes market orientation across an organisation?

B. Sharing customer and competitor insight to coordinate delivery of value

A Customer experience depends on operations, finance, service and other functions as well as marketing. Sole departmental responsibility weakens the coordination needed to fulfil the organisation's promises.

B · correct Market orientation combines customer understanding, competitor understanding and coordinated action across functions. Shared insight matters because the whole organisation contributes to the value customers actually receive.

C Promotional volume measures activity rather than whether the organisation understands and serves customers. A market-oriented culture connects decisions and delivery to customer value and longer-term performance.

D Product expertise is useful, but market orientation also requires evidence about customers and alternatives. Internal opinions alone cannot establish which benefits matter in the buying context.

Revisit lesson 3: A market-oriented organisation
Q006 · Lesson 3 · applicationReturn to question

A retailer advertises reliable collection, but orders are often unavailable when customers arrive. Which response best supports market orientation?

A. Align stock planning, collection procedures and customer communications around the promise

A · correct The failure spans the promise and its delivery. Coordinating stock, operations and communication addresses the customer experience and makes the advertised benefit more consistently achievable.

B Greater advertising frequency may attract more customers to an unreliable service. Awareness cannot resolve the underlying coordination failure between the promised collection experience and actual availability.

C Stronger promises increase expectations without improving fulfilment. Market orientation requires sales and operations to agree on commitments that the organisation can deliver reliably for customers.

D Campaign reach may help evaluate promotion, but it does not explain unavailable orders. The immediate evidence points to delivery processes that directly undermine the promised customer value.

Revisit lesson 3: A market-oriented organisation
Part 02 · Understand every option

Q007-Q009 · Reasoning

Q007 · Lesson 4 · foundationReturn to question

Which opening statement gives a marketing plan the clearest scope?

D. The plan addresses repeat purchases of one range among a defined segment over twelve months

A Success is too broad to define the planning decision. A useful scope identifies the offer, priority customer group, market and period that recommendations will address.

B History and stakeholders provide context, but this statement does not delimit the decision. The plan still needs a specified offer, customer group and planning period.

C Naming models describes potential analytical tools rather than the planning problem. Models should follow a clear scope so their findings address a relevant business decision.

D · correct This statement identifies the offer, priority customer group, intended behaviour and time horizon. Those boundaries make it easier to select relevant evidence and develop focused recommendations.

Revisit lesson 4: Start the plan with context
Q008 · Lesson 4 · applicationReturn to question

Rehab is planning a city-based stationery delivery service. She has limited space for the organisation background. Which fact is most relevant to include?

C. The current delivery capacity within the proposed service area

A An incorporation date can provide context, but no connection to the current decision is stated. Delivery capacity directly constrains the proposed service and deserves priority in this brief.

B Office history may explain capabilities in some cases, but an exhaustive account is unnecessary here. Background should prioritise evidence that affects the current planning decision.

C · correct Delivery capacity determines how many customers the service can reach and serve reliably. It directly informs feasible objectives, resources and the geographic scope of the plan.

D Past awards may support reputation when they are relevant to the current offer. Awards for an unrelated discontinued product provide less direct planning evidence than present delivery capacity.

Revisit lesson 4: Start the plan with context
Q009 · Lesson 5 · foundationReturn to question

Which portfolio dimension describes how closely a company's product lines relate to one another?

A. Consistency

A · correct Consistency concerns relationships among product lines, such as shared uses, customers or production requirements. It describes their connection rather than counting lines, items or variants.

B Width counts the number of product lines in the mix. It does not indicate whether those lines share customers, production processes, distribution channels or uses.

C Length counts the total product items across the mix under the chosen convention. It does not measure how closely the company's different product lines relate.

D Depth concerns the variants offered for a product item, such as sizes or fragrances. It does not describe the relationship between the company's product lines.

Revisit lesson 5: Describe the business & its portfolio
Part 02 · Understand every option

Q010-Q012 · Reasoning

Q010 · Lesson 5 · applicationReturn to question

A business defines its mix as three product lines containing eight product items in total. One item has four size variants. Under this counting convention, what are width, length and that item's depth?

C. Width 3, length 8, depth 4

A This reverses width and length. The three lines establish width, while the eight defined product items establish length; four sizes describe the depth of one item.

B The scenario defines variants separately from product items, so adding four sizes to the eight items changes the counting convention. Length remains eight under the stated definition.

C · correct Width counts three lines, length counts eight product items, and depth counts four variants of the specified item. Keeping the stated counting convention prevents mixing these dimensions.

D The four sizes are variants of one item, not four product lines. The business has three lines, so width is three and the item's depth is four.

Revisit lesson 5: Describe the business & its portfolio
Q011 · Lesson 6 · foundationReturn to question

How do the BCG matrix and product life cycle differ?

D. BCG compares growth and relative share; the life cycle describes possible development over time

A BCG uses market growth and relative market share, not product age. Life-cycle discussion concerns development over time, but age alone cannot establish a product's stage.

B BCG positions do not directly measure profitability; costs and investment still matter. The life cycle describes possible sales development rather than serving as a market-share measure.

C BCG quadrants and life-cycle stages answer different questions and are not interchangeable. A long-established product can still hold low share in a market experiencing high growth.

D · correct BCG compares a product's portfolio position using market growth and relative share. The life cycle helps discuss how sales and profit may evolve without prescribing a fixed path.

Revisit lesson 6: Portfolio choices: BCG & product life cycle
Q012 · Lesson 6 · applicationReturn to question

In an illustrative high-growth market, a product has 18% share and its largest competitor has 30%. Treat relative share below 1.0 as low. Which assessment is correct?

B. Relative share 0.60; question mark

A Dividing the competitor's share by the product's share reverses the ratio. Relative share is 18 divided by 30, so the product falls below the stated high-share threshold.

B · correct Relative market share is 18 divided by 30, or 0.60. Low relative share combined with the specified high market growth places the product in the question-mark quadrant.

C The ratio is correct, but a cash cow combines high relative share with low market growth. This product has low relative share in a high-growth market.

D Twelve is the percentage-point gap between the shares, not their ratio. A dog or pet also requires low market growth, contrary to the scenario's stated condition.

Revisit lesson 6: Portfolio choices: BCG & product life cycle
Part 02 · Understand every option

Q013-Q015 · Reasoning

Q013 · Lesson 7 · foundationReturn to question

A supplier sells office furniture directly to a government department. Which customer-market label is most specific?

C. B2G

A B2C describes sales to consumers for their personal use. Here the purchasing customer is a government department, so the more specific market label is B2G.

B Recruitment markets concern obtaining employees or skills needed by the organisation. This transaction concerns a government buyer purchasing furniture, rather than a business recruiting staff.

C · correct B2G describes selling to government buyers. The department is purchasing furniture for organisational use, making this label more specific than a general description of business customers.

D A referral market concerns people or organisations that recommend an offer. The government department is the direct purchaser in this scenario, not merely a source of recommendations.

Revisit lesson 7: Map customers, competitors & stakeholders
Q014 · Lesson 7 · applicationReturn to question

A wholesaler buys a manufacturer's products and also manages deliveries to retailers. How should the manufacturer map this relationship?

D. As both a customer and delivery partner, recording the implications of each role

A Purchasing makes the wholesaler a customer, but it also performs delivery activities. Ignoring that second role would hide a dependency that affects availability and customer experience.

B Delivery creates an operational relationship, but the wholesaler also buys products. Mapping only one role would miss the commercial interest and influence associated with its purchasing decisions.

C The roles belong to the same organisation, so their interests and dependencies may interact. Treating them as unrelated would obscure how commercial decisions can affect delivery.

D · correct One stakeholder can perform several relevant roles. Recording both purchasing and fulfilment responsibilities reveals how its interests, influence and performance affect the manufacturer's marketing promise.

Revisit lesson 7: Map customers, competitors & stakeholders
Q015 · Lesson 8 · foundationReturn to question

Within SOSTAC, which activity belongs most directly to Control?

B. Comparing repeat-purchase results with targets and triggering adjustments

A Selecting the target segment and competitive approach belongs mainly to Strategy. Control evaluates performance against objectives and uses the evidence to decide whether adjustments are needed.

B · correct Control measures progress against intended outcomes and supports corrective decisions. Comparing repeat-purchase results with targets links the plan's delivery to evidence about whether it is working.

C Assigning owners belongs mainly to Action, which specifies who does what and when. Control instead monitors outcomes and identifies whether the plan requires a response.

D Choosing promotional channels belongs mainly to Tactics, where the marketing mix is specified. Control then assesses whether those choices contribute to the objectives of the plan.

Revisit lesson 8: SOSTAC: the spine of the plan
Part 02 · Understand every option

Q016-Q018 · Reasoning

Q016 · Lesson 8 · applicationReturn to question

A team creates a SWOT list entirely from opinions and immediately selects campaigns. What is the most useful next step?

A. Validate internal and external evidence before using SWOT to develop strategic options

A · correct SWOT should summarise supported internal and external findings. Validating the audit first gives the team a credible basis for developing options through combinations such as TOWS.

B More tactics do not resolve the weak evidence beneath the SWOT. The team should first test its assumptions about resources, customers, competition and wider environmental conditions.

C Budget constraints matter, but selecting expenditure before validating the situation can commit resources to an unsupported direction. Audit evidence should inform objectives, strategy and subsequent tactical choices.

D An opportunity is an interpretation of external evidence, not proof that customers want a particular offer. The team must examine relevance and feasibility before selecting its response.

Revisit lesson 8: SOSTAC: the spine of the plan
Q017 · Lesson 9 · foundationReturn to question

Which factor belongs most clearly in the macro environment rather than the immediate micro environment?

A. A broad increase in market interest rates

A · correct Market interest rates are a broad economic condition affecting financing and demand across organisations. They belong in macro analysis, although the specific impact varies by business.

B A named rival's product launch concerns the competitive environment close to the business. It belongs primarily in micro analysis rather than describing a broad macroeconomic condition.

C A distributor's order schedule concerns a direct market relationship and operational dependency. It sits in the micro environment, even when wider economic conditions influence the distributor.

D A customer's discount request concerns an immediate buyer relationship. Macro conditions may help explain it, but the request itself is part of the business's micro environment.

Revisit lesson 9: PESTEL: political & economic forces
Q018 · Lesson 9 · applicationReturn to question

In an illustrative market, financing costs rise and a furniture retailer depends heavily on installment purchases. Which PESTEL conclusion is best supported?

C. Costlier installments may weaken affordability, so assess exposure and test feasible responses

A Higher financing costs can make installment purchases less affordable, rather than automatically increasing demand. The effect depends on customer incomes, alternatives and the retailer's specific exposure.

B An interest-rate change is an external economic condition, not an internal strength. Its implications should be assessed through the retailer's financing arrangements and target customers' purchasing behaviour.

C · correct This conclusion explains a plausible route from a macroeconomic change to customer affordability. It also recognises that the retailer needs exposure evidence before choosing and testing a response.

D A rate change alone cannot determine an exact sales decline. Customer sensitivity, pricing, financing terms, competing offers and category priorities can all influence the eventual demand response.

Revisit lesson 9: PESTEL: political & economic forces
Part 02 · Understand every option

Q019-Q021 · Reasoning

Q019 · Lesson 10 · foundationReturn to question

Why should demographic analysis examine income distribution as well as average income?

D. An average can conceal substantial differences between customer groups

A Average income summarises a population and does not reveal each household's commitments or spending capacity. Distribution and relevant segment evidence provide a more useful picture of affordability.

B Income distribution can help describe differences, but the business still needs to define and understand its target. Income alone does not establish needs, behaviour or reachability.

C Income averages do not reveal individual preferences or purchase criteria. Research into customer context and behaviour remains necessary to understand the benefits a target group values.

D · correct A population average can rise while some groups experience little improvement. Examining distribution helps determine whether the target segment shares in the change and can afford the offer.

Revisit lesson 10: Economic exposure & social change
Q020 · Lesson 10 · applicationReturn to question

A report from another country suggests that busy households favour scheduled deliveries. A local retailer wants to invest in this service. What should it do first?

B. Test the proposed benefit with its local target segment and purchase evidence

A A foreign finding can suggest a hypothesis, but customer circumstances and infrastructure may differ. Local evidence is needed before assuming the same demand and service priorities apply.

B · correct Research with the defined local segment can test whether time pressure creates demand for scheduled delivery. Purchase evidence helps connect stated preferences with actual behaviour and potential uptake.

C Households differ in schedules, responsibilities and shopping habits. Treating the whole area as uniform would overlook which customers value the service and what delivery arrangements they need.

D The report concerns convenience and timing, not a demonstrated desire for more products. Expanding variety would require separate evidence connecting that change to the target customers' needs.

Revisit lesson 10: Economic exposure & social change
Q021 · Lesson 11 · foundationReturn to question

Which customer journey is an example of webrooming?

C. Researching a product online before purchasing it in a shop

A Inspecting in a physical shop and then buying online is showrooming. Webrooming reverses that research-to-purchase sequence by moving from online investigation to a store transaction.

B An entirely online purchase does not include the store transaction that defines webrooming. The distinction concerns how research and purchasing connect across online and physical channels.

C · correct Webrooming begins with online research and ends with an in-store purchase. It highlights the need to connect digital information with physical availability and the store experience.

D A journey contained within a physical shop does not involve online research. Webrooming specifically links digital investigation with a later purchase through a physical retail outlet.

Revisit lesson 11: Technology, environment & buying journeys
Part 02 · Understand every option

Q022-Q024 · Reasoning

Q022 · Lesson 11 · applicationReturn to question

A manager uses a technology's position on Gartner's Hype Cycle to claim the company can forecast next year's product sales. What is the strongest response?

A. Use it to discuss expectations and maturity, then assess demand through separate market evidence

A · correct The Hype Cycle concerns expectations and technology maturity rather than product sales. Demand forecasting still needs evidence about customers, adoption, the offer and the relevant market context.

B Knowing the price does not turn an expectations framework into a sales model. Sales also depend on demand, access, competition and the organisation's ability to deliver value.

C Technologies at similar maturity stages can address very different markets and needs. Their shared position on the framework does not establish equivalent adoption, revenue or sales volumes.

D Publicity can influence expectations but does not prove customer demand or practical usefulness. Customer and market evidence remain necessary when assessing whether a technology supports a viable offer.

Revisit lesson 11: Technology, environment & buying journeys
Q023 · Lesson 12 · foundationReturn to question

What makes an environmental-audit entry useful for a marketing decision?

B. Dated evidence linked to impact, timing, implications and a proposed response

A A list can identify topics for investigation, but it does not explain their relevance. Decision-useful analysis connects evidence with exposure, timing, likely effects and an appropriate response.

B · correct A useful entry shows both the evidence and its implications for the organisation. Timing and a proposed response connect environmental observation with choices in the marketing plan.

C A label alone does not show why a factor helps or harms the business. The analysis needs evidence about exposure and may identify both opportunities and threats.

D A general trend has limited planning value without a link to the organisation. The audit must explain which customers, costs, capabilities or decisions are likely to be affected.

Revisit lesson 12: Make the environmental audit actionable
Q024 · Lesson 12 · applicationReturn to question

In an invented planning case, a proposed packaging requirement could raise redesign costs next year and make product information clearer. How should the audit record it?

D. As a factor with possible costs and benefits, supported by evidence, timing and uncertainty

A The scenario includes a potential cost and a potential customer benefit. Recording only a threat would miss the opportunity to improve information while planning for redesign expenditure.

B Clearer information may improve the customer experience, but it does not remove redesign costs. The audit should consider both effects when assessing the organisation's response and resources.

C A proposal is not the same as a confirmed immediate requirement. Recording its status, expected timing and uncertainty supports proportionate planning and avoids presenting assumptions as established facts.

D · correct A single external factor can create both upside and downside. Recording evidence, timing and uncertainty helps the organisation assess costs, customer value and an appropriate response.

Revisit lesson 12: Make the environmental audit actionable
Part 02 · Understand every option

Q025-Q027 · Reasoning

Q025 · Lesson 13 · foundationReturn to question

Which condition is most likely to create a barrier to entering an industry?

D. New firms need substantial capital and difficult-to-obtain distribution access

A Easy comparison can affect buyer power and rivalry, but it does not by itself prevent firms from entering. Entry barriers concern obstacles to establishing a viable operation.

B High closure costs are exit barriers that can keep existing firms competing despite weak returns. They differ from the obstacles a new entrant must overcome to begin operating.

C Slow demand growth can intensify rivalry for existing customers. It may discourage entry commercially, but the stated capital and distribution obstacles more directly constitute entry barriers.

D · correct Capital requirements and restricted distribution access make it harder to establish a credible competing operation. Both can reduce the threat of new entrants from an incumbent's perspective.

Revisit lesson 13: Rivalry & barriers to entry
Q026 · Lesson 13 · applicationReturn to question

A proposed manufacturer must fund specialised equipment and complete lengthy certification before selling. From an incumbent's perspective, which judgement is best supported?

C. These requirements can reduce entry pressure, although other competitive forces still require analysis

A Entry barriers concern new competitors, while rivalry concerns firms already operating. Existing manufacturers may still compete intensely through price, service, advertising or capacity despite difficult entry.

B Barriers can protect incumbents from some entrants, but they do not guarantee profit or permanence. Buyer power, substitutes, supplier pressure and existing rivalry can still affect returns.

C · correct Large investment and lengthy certification raise the difficulty of entering. They support a judgement of lower entry pressure while leaving the other forces to be assessed separately.

D Certification concerns a manufacturer's ability to enter the industry. Customer switching costs concern the burdens of changing provider, which require different evidence about the buying relationship.

Revisit lesson 13: Rivalry & barriers to entry
Q027 · Lesson 14 · foundationReturn to question

A rail operator defines its industry as intercity rail travel. Which offer is most clearly a substitute satisfying the same underlying customer need?

A. An intercity coach service connecting the same destinations

A · correct A coach service can satisfy the same need for intercity travel through a different mode. Under the stated rail-industry boundary, it is a substitute rather than a rail rival.

B Another rail company competes within the defined industry and is therefore a direct rival. A substitute meets the underlying travel need through a different type of solution.

C A component supplier provides an input to rail operations rather than an alternative way for customers to travel. Its influence belongs primarily in analysis of supplier power.

D A booking system supports the rail service but does not itself transport the customer. It is not an alternative solution to the underlying need for intercity travel.

Revisit lesson 14: Switching costs, substitutes & suppliers
Part 02 · Understand every option

Q028-Q030 · Reasoning

Q028 · Lesson 14 · applicationReturn to question

A café depends on one specialist ingredient supplier. Two alternatives appear, but neither can meet its quality standard or delivery volume. How should the café assess supplier power?

B. It may remain strong because the alternatives are not currently suitable

A Counting names overstates the café's options when alternatives cannot meet essential requirements. Bargaining power depends on credible alternatives and feasible switching, not simply the number of listed suppliers.

B · correct Alternatives weaken dependence only when they can supply suitable quality and capacity. The café still lacks a credible replacement, so the incumbent supplier may retain substantial bargaining power.

C A supplier can possess bargaining power without exercising it through a price increase. The café's dependence and lack of suitable alternatives matter when assessing potential negotiating leverage.

D Delivery capacity determines whether an alternative can credibly replace the incumbent. It therefore affects the café's ability to switch and is directly relevant to the supplier's bargaining power.

Revisit lesson 14: Switching costs, substitutes & suppliers
Q029 · Lesson 15 · foundationReturn to question

Which action represents backward integration by a furniture manufacturer?

C. Acquiring a business that supplies its timber

A Opening shops moves the manufacturer toward distribution and end customers, which is forward integration. Backward integration moves in the opposite direction, toward activities that provide inputs.

B Buying a competing manufacturer expands activity at the same stage of the supply chain. Backward integration instead moves toward a supplier or another source of production inputs.

C · correct Timber is an input to furniture production, so acquiring its supplier moves the manufacturer backward along the supply chain. This can alter dependence and require additional operating capabilities.

D A complementary service can improve customer value through partnership, but the described arrangement does not acquire an input supplier. It therefore does not demonstrate backward integration.

Revisit lesson 15: Buyer power, integration & complements
Q030 · Lesson 15 · applicationReturn to question

An e-reader producer works with publishers to expand the range of compatible books. Which interpretation best explains the publishers' role?

D. They are complementers because their content makes the device more useful

A Compatible books and the e-reader are used together in this scenario. The relevant relationship adds value to the device rather than replacing the need it serves.

B Releasing compatible content does not mean a publisher has entered device production. Entry analysis depends on the defined industry and what competitive activity the organisation actually undertakes.

C A stronger content offer may improve adoption, but it does not remove rivals, substitutes or bargaining pressures. Complementary relationships can also create dependencies that require management.

D · correct Compatible books make owning the e-reader more valuable, so publishers act as complementers. The partnership can support adoption while also creating relationships and dependencies worth assessing.

Revisit lesson 15: Buyer power, integration & complements
Part 02 · Understand every option

Q031-Q033 · Reasoning

Q031 · Lesson 16 · foundationReturn to question

What should determine the dimensions selected for a customer perceptual map?

B. Evidence about dimensions that matter in customers' buying decisions

A Advertising priorities may reflect the company's ambitions rather than customers' decision criteria. A perceptual map needs meaningful customer dimensions and researched positions to support useful interpretation.

B · correct The map should use dimensions customers consider meaningful when choosing among alternatives. Research then establishes perceived positions, allowing the organisation to compare its intended and actual image.

C Choosing axes to manufacture an empty space can create a misleading opportunity. The dimensions should first reflect meaningful customer criteria, and any apparent gap still needs commercial testing.

D Internal scores describe the company's own assessment, which may differ from customer perceptions. Selecting favourable attributes can hide the real competitive picture the map should reveal.

Revisit lesson 16: Competitor analysis & perceptual maps
Q032 · Lesson 16 · applicationReturn to question

A delivery firm calls its service premium, but customer research places it near competitors on perceived reliability. What is the best next step?

A. Investigate delivery and communication evidence to understand and address the perception gap

A · correct The research identifies a gap between the intended position and perceived performance. Investigating delivery and communication can show whether the firm needs operational improvement, clearer evidence or repositioning.

B Changing the point to match management's preference would replace research with aspiration. The map should record customer perceptions so the organisation can identify and investigate discrepancies.

C Customers may not observe every process, but their experience shapes perceived reliability and choice. Discarding their responses removes evidence directly relevant to the firm's intended market position.

D Price may signal quality, but it does not automatically change service performance or customer beliefs. A credible reliability position needs delivery and supporting evidence that customers value.

Revisit lesson 16: Competitor analysis & perceptual maps
Q033 · Lesson 17 · foundationReturn to question

Which statement best distinguishes an organisational capability from a resource?

D. A capability is an ability to use resources to perform consistently

A Equipment is a resource that may support performance, but ownership alone does not establish a capability. Skills, systems and processes determine whether it can be used effectively.

B Purchase price does not establish an ability to deliver value. An expensive resource may remain ineffective if staff lack the skills, incentives or processes needed to use it.

C Capabilities can exist across operations, service, finance and other functions. Marketing performance often depends on combining resources and coordinated activity throughout the organisation rather than one department.

D · correct Capabilities concern what the organisation can repeatedly do with its resources. The distinction explains why possessing assets does not automatically produce reliable delivery or superior customer value.

Revisit lesson 17: Audit the organisation from the inside
Part 02 · Understand every option

Q034-Q036 · Reasoning

Q034 · Lesson 17 · applicationReturn to question

A training company has skilled tutors and strong course material, but sales and scheduling teams do not share updates. Customers repeatedly receive incorrect start dates. What does the internal audit indicate?

B. Poor communication prevents useful resources from producing consistent customer value

A Tutor expertise is a useful resource, but customers also depend on accurate scheduling. Repeated date errors show that the combined delivery capability has a significant organisational weakness.

B · correct The resources have potential value, but weak coordination undermines delivery. Sharing accurate updates across teams is part of turning expertise and material into a consistent customer experience.

C The stated cause is an internal communication failure, not a broad economic condition. Internal audit examines how processes, collaboration and resources support or obstruct the chosen strategy.

D Additional material does not address inaccurate scheduling information. The audit should connect the observed customer failure to its organisational cause before recommending further investment in resources.

Revisit lesson 17: Audit the organisation from the inside
Q035 · Lesson 18 · foundationReturn to question

Which resource is generally an intangible asset?

A. A patent protecting a production method

A · correct A patent is an intellectual property right rather than a physical object. It may support technology and advantage, but it is generally classified as an intangible asset.

B A warehouse is a physical facility and therefore a tangible resource. Its location, capacity and condition can still have important implications for delivery and customer value.

C A delivery vehicle is a physical asset used in operations, so it is tangible. Its strategic value depends on condition, availability and fit with the distribution requirement.

D A packaging machine is physical equipment and therefore a tangible resource. The patent or software rights supporting a process would be conceptually different from the machine itself.

Revisit lesson 18: Resources: visible assets & hidden strengths
Q036 · Lesson 18 · applicationReturn to question

A business lists a large warehouse as a strength. Its growth plan depends on rapid city deliveries, but the warehouse is remote and often inaccessible. How should the resource be assessed?

C. Against delivery requirements, availability and relevant benchmarks before judging its value

A Size alone does not establish strategic usefulness. A remote or inaccessible warehouse may undermine the speed and reliability required by the plan despite offering substantial storage capacity.

B Physical resources directly affect distribution and service delivery. Financial capacity matters, but it cannot replace assessment of whether the warehouse supports the particular customer promise and growth strategy.

C · correct Resource assessment should examine quality, availability and relevance to the strategy. Delivery requirements and meaningful benchmarks reveal whether the warehouse supports rapid service or creates a constraint.

D Owning a facility does not demonstrate the ability to distribute reliably. Location, access, processes and complementary resources determine whether warehouse capacity becomes an effective delivery capability.

Revisit lesson 18: Resources: visible assets & hidden strengths
Part 02 · Understand every option

Q037-Q039 · Reasoning

Q037 · Lesson 19 · foundationReturn to question

What does the final letter in VRIO add to the resource assessment?

B. Whether the organisation is arranged to exploit the resource

A Non-substitutability is the final consideration in VRIN. VRIO instead asks whether organisational arrangements, such as systems and incentives, allow the business to exploit the resource effectively.

B · correct The organisation question examines whether people, systems and incentives enable effective use. A valuable, rare resource can remain underused when the business lacks the arrangements to exploit it.

C Age alone does not demonstrate organisation or advantage. VRIO examines whether the firm can exploit a valuable resource, not simply how long it has owned or developed it.

D A resource need not suit every target market to be strategically useful. The organisation question asks whether the business can exploit it within the strategy it has chosen.

Revisit lesson 19: From resources to advantage: VRIN & VRIO
Q038 · Lesson 19 · applicationReturn to question

A retailer introduces a useful service process that competitors can observe and copy cheaply within weeks. Which VRIN assessment is most defensible?

D. The process may be valuable, but easy imitation weakens its potential for lasting advantage

A Value and non-substitutability are separate questions. Customers appreciating the process does not establish that another resource or approach could not deliver a similar benefit for them.

B Being first may create a temporary distinction, but cheap copying can quickly remove rarity. The scenario directly limits any claim that the process will remain difficult to match.

C Value is necessary for strategic usefulness, but VRIN also examines rarity, imitation and substitutes. A benefit competitors can reproduce cheaply does not establish a lasting advantage by itself.

D · correct The process can benefit customers while remaining easy for rivals to imitate. That weakness limits claims of lasting advantage and suggests examining additional resources or capabilities that are harder to copy.

Revisit lesson 19: From resources to advantage: VRIN & VRIO
Q039 · Lesson 20 · foundationReturn to question

Which statement is the most complete measurable marketing objective, assuming feasibility has been supported?

C. The retention team will raise six-month repeat purchase from 30% to 36% for Cairo customers by June

A Admiration and better marketing are not defined through a metric, baseline or deadline. An objective needs a specific result that the organisation can assess within a stated period.

B This specifies an activity and timing, but not the customer or business outcome it should achieve. A measurable outcome objective explains what improvement the campaigns are intended to support.

C · correct This identifies an owner, customer group, metric, baseline, target and deadline. With feasibility supported as stated, it provides a specific result that can be monitored and evaluated.

D Focusing on existing customers describes a strategic choice rather than a measurable destination. The plan still needs a defined outcome, baseline, target and deadline to assess progress.

Revisit lesson 20: SMART objectives & growth direction
Part 02 · Understand every option

Q040-Q042 · Reasoning

Q040 · Lesson 20 · applicationReturn to question

An illustrative objective raises market share from 20% to 25% in the same defined market. What is the increase in percentage points and the relative percentage increase?

A. 5 percentage points; 25% relative increase

A · correct Subtracting 20 from 25 gives a five-percentage-point increase. Dividing that change by the initial share gives 5 divided by 20, which equals a 25% relative increase.

B Five is the percentage-point change, not the relative percentage increase. Relative growth compares the change with the initial 20% share, giving 5 divided by 20, or 25%.

C The final market share is 25%, but the change is only five percentage points. Relative growth uses the initial 20% as the denominator, producing a 25% increase.

D Twenty is the starting share rather than the percentage-point change. The relative increase is correctly calculated as 25%, but the absolute difference between the shares is five points.

Revisit lesson 20: SMART objectives & growth direction
Q041 · Lesson 21 · foundationReturn to question

How does Porter's generic-strategy analysis complement Ansoff's matrix?

D. It clarifies the basis of competitive advantage alongside the direction of growth

A A promotional schedule belongs to tactics and action planning. Generic strategies address how the business competes, while Ansoff distinguishes growth directions using products and markets.

B Both frameworks still require a defined business and market context. Porter helps assess the basis of advantage, but it does not remove the need to understand target customers.

C Neither framework guarantees profitability or assigns a fixed return to new products. Results depend on market conditions, customer value, organisational capabilities and the economics of implementation.

D · correct Ansoff distinguishes existing and new products and markets, while Porter examines competitive advantage. Using both connects the chosen growth direction with a reason customers should prefer the business.

Revisit lesson 21: Where to grow & how to compete
Q042 · Lesson 21 · applicationReturn to question

A software company currently serves hotels only. It offers its unchanged scheduling product to dental practices, a customer market new to the business. Which Ansoff direction fits the stated definitions?

C. Market development

A Penetration uses existing products in existing markets. The product is unchanged, but dental practices are explicitly a new customer market for the company, so penetration does not fit.

B Product development introduces a new product to an existing market. This scenario specifies the opposite combination: the software remains unchanged while the company addresses a new customer market.

C · correct Market development uses an existing product in a market new to the business. The unchanged scheduling software and newly targeted dental practices match those two stated conditions.

D Diversification requires both a new product and a new market under the chosen definitions. Although the customer market changes here, the scenario explicitly keeps the product unchanged.

Revisit lesson 21: Where to grow & how to compete
Part 02 · Understand every option

Q043-Q045 · Reasoning

Q043 · Lesson 22 · foundationReturn to question

A business serves a narrow segment through a sustainably lower cost base. Which generic strategy best describes this combination?

A. Cost focus

A · correct Cost focus combines a narrow competitive scope with lower cost as the source of advantage. Both elements are specified, distinguishing it from broad cost leadership and differentiation strategies.

B Broad differentiation combines a wide target market with a valued distinctive offer. The scenario instead specifies a narrow segment and lower cost as the basis of advantage.

C Differentiation focus does address a narrow segment, but its advantage comes from a valued difference. Here the stated source of advantage is a sustainably lower cost base.

D Broad cost leadership shares the lower-cost basis but serves a wide market. The narrow segment in this scenario makes cost focus the more accurate description of the strategy.

Revisit lesson 22: Scope, advantage & meaningful difference
Q044 · Lesson 22 · applicationReturn to question

A luggage brand can add either an unusual decorative badge or a reliable repair service. Target-customer research values repair support, and the service can be delivered economically. Which choice best supports meaningful differentiation?

B. Develop the repair service and support the promise with dependable delivery

A Uniqueness alone does not establish a meaningful difference. The badge lacks stated customer value, while the repair service has evidence of relevance, feasibility and an acceptable economic basis.

B · correct The repair service meets the key tests: customers value it, the business can deliver it and the economics work. Reliable execution makes the differentiation credible in the actual experience.

C Ease of communication can help promotion, but it does not establish customer value. The repair service has stronger evidence that its difference matters and can be delivered economically.

D Adding an untested feature can increase cost or complexity without strengthening preference. The evidence supports repair service, while the badge needs its own justification before inclusion in the offer.

Revisit lesson 22: Scope, advantage & meaningful difference
Q045 · Lesson 23 · foundationReturn to question

Which sequence correctly describes STP?

C. Identify meaningful groups, choose whom to serve, then define the intended reason to choose

A Starting with a message before understanding customer differences reverses the STP logic. Segmentation and targeting should inform the position and the message used to communicate it.

B Price and distribution are marketing-mix decisions that follow strategic choices. STP specifically concerns segmentation, targeting and positioning rather than a sequence of selected tactical decisions alone.

C · correct Segmentation identifies meaningful differences, targeting selects groups to serve, and positioning defines the intended reason to choose the offer. These choices then guide a coherent marketing mix.

D Competitor evidence can inform strategy, but copying and maximising reach do not constitute STP. The process requires meaningful customer groups, a target choice and a relevant position.

Revisit lesson 23: STP & demographic segmentation
Part 02 · Understand every option

Q046-Q048 · Reasoning

Q046 · Lesson 23 · applicationReturn to question

A meal-kit business finds that customers of the same age divide between those seeking quick preparation and those seeking new cooking experiences. What is the most useful segmentation response?

D. Combine age with benefits sought and behaviour when these differences improve decisions

A The research already shows different needs among customers of the same age. Using age alone would conceal distinctions that could change the offer, communication and service experience.

B Different preferences within an age group are plausible and strategically useful. The business should examine their consistency and relevance rather than dismissing them because they challenge a demographic assumption.

C Narrower age bands do not necessarily explain the observed preferences. Any segmentation variable should be tested for whether it helps identify meaningful needs or different responses to the offer.

D · correct Combining relevant variables can produce more useful segments than age alone. Benefits and behaviour directly connect the observed differences with decisions about preparation time, recipes and communications.

Revisit lesson 23: STP & demographic segmentation
Q047 · Lesson 24 · foundationReturn to question

How should a traditional family-life-cycle model be used in segmentation?

B. As a set of possible situations whose relevance needs evidence

A Households follow many different paths, including arrangements omitted by traditional models. Treating the stages as compulsory would hide real variation in circumstances and potential customer needs.

B · correct The model can suggest how responsibilities and priorities might change, but real households vary. Research should establish which situations matter and what they imply for the specific buying decision.

C Marriage does not establish the number of earners or the level of financial commitments. Disposable income must be assessed through relevant evidence rather than inferred from a life-stage label.

D The model provides possible research prompts, not a substitute for customer evidence. Responsibilities, time pressures and spending priorities still need investigation within the defined target market.

Revisit lesson 24: Life stage, income & occupation
Q048 · Lesson 24 · applicationReturn to question

A subscription business labels a segment "newly married" and assumes every household has two incomes and ample leisure time. What should it change first?

A. Research earners, commitments and routines before designing the offer

A · correct The label does not establish income or available time. Research into household commitments and routines provides a sounder basis for deciding which benefits, prices and service arrangements fit.

B Newly married households do not necessarily have high disposable income. Premium-only offers based on the label risk ignoring different earnings, commitments and priorities within the group.

C Age can provide context, but it does not directly measure household routines or time pressure. The business needs evidence about responsibilities and behaviour relevant to the subscription.

D Extending unsupported assumptions broadens the error rather than improving segmentation. Households differ in structure and circumstances, so the business should investigate relevant variation before generalising its offer.

Revisit lesson 24: Life stage, income & occupation
Part 02 · Understand every option

Q049-Q051 · Reasoning

Q049 · Lesson 25 · foundationReturn to question

What is the main limitation of using a generational label to predict buying behaviour?

D. It can hide differences within the group and confuse several sources of behaviour

A A generational label groups people historically; it does not measure an individual's motives. Buying behaviour still needs evidence about goals, context, preferences and the category being considered.

B Generational boundaries vary across sources, so the label does not guarantee a consistent definition. Researchers should state their grouping and avoid treating it as a universal behavioural explanation.

C A label alone cannot distinguish historical cohort influences from age or current circumstances. That distinction requires more careful evidence than simply assigning customers to a named generation.

D · correct People within a generation differ, and observed behaviour may reflect age or present circumstances. Labels can organise research but should not replace evidence about the customers being studied.

Revisit lesson 25: Use demographic labels with evidence
Q050 · Lesson 25 · applicationReturn to question

A travel retailer expects customers of one nationality to prefer the same language and holiday style. Which research approach best improves this assumption?

C. Test language needs and travel preferences within the defined group, allowing for variation

A Nationality may provide context but does not establish uniform preferences. Applying the assumption to every customer would overlook differences in language, experience, purpose and desired travel benefits.

B Product assignment needs evidence about the customer's requirements and buying context. Nationality alone cannot establish the combination of language support, destination and holiday experience that someone values.

C · correct Testing specific needs turns a demographic assumption into a research question. Allowing variation within the group helps the retailer identify useful patterns without treating the label as a complete explanation.

D Changing demographic labels does not solve unsupported certainty. A generational category also contains varied needs, so the retailer still needs direct evidence about relevant preferences and travel circumstances.

Revisit lesson 25: Use demographic labels with evidence
Q051 · Lesson 26 · foundationReturn to question

Which variable is most clearly psychographic?

A. A preference for self-expression and trying unfamiliar experiences

A · correct Self-expression and openness to unfamiliar experiences concern motives, values and lifestyle. These psychological patterns can help explain why customers with similar demographic profiles choose differently in a category.

B Household size is a demographic descriptor rather than a direct measure of motives or lifestyle. It may influence needs, but the relevant psychological explanation still requires research.

C A postcode is a geographic variable indicating location. It may correlate with other characteristics, but it does not directly describe the customer's values, motivations or interests.

D Age is a demographic variable rather than a psychographic one. People of the same age can differ substantially in values, interests, motives and preferred ways of living.

Revisit lesson 26: Psychographics, personas & VALS
Part 02 · Understand every option

Q052-Q054 · Reasoning

Q052 · Lesson 26 · applicationReturn to question

Research finds a recurring group that compares evidence carefully and abandons purchases when terms are unclear. Which persona detail would be most useful for the marketing team?

B. A need for credible comparisons and clear terms, linked to content and support choices

A An unrelated invented preference adds biography without improving a marketing decision. Useful personas prioritise researched goals, barriers and criteria that can guide the offer and customer experience.

B · correct This detail captures a researched decision pattern and connects it to action. Comparisons, transparent terms and support address the group's observed criteria and reasons for abandoning purchases.

C A photograph can make a persona memorable, but it does not explain buying behaviour. The decision-relevant content should come from evidence about needs, barriers and purchase criteria.

D Estimated income alone cannot establish a validated VALS type. A useful persona should represent observed patterns rather than converting a limited demographic estimate into an unsupported psychological classification.

Revisit lesson 26: Psychographics, personas & VALS
Q053 · Lesson 27 · foundationReturn to question

When applying the lesson's Innovator and Survivor profiles, what does the term "resources" require us to recognise?

C. Relevant resources extend beyond money, so income alone cannot establish a profile

A The lesson explicitly treats resources as broader than money. Income can contribute context, but it cannot by itself establish motivations, confidence, preferences or a validated customer profile.

B Profiles describe tendencies within a framework rather than fixed individual behaviour. Resources and buying context need investigation, and the same person may approach different purchases in different ways.

C · correct Financial means are only part of the relevant picture. Applying the framework carefully requires psychological and behavioural evidence, so an income figure alone is insufficient to establish a profile.

D Equal income does not establish equal motivations or receptiveness to change. Customers can differ in confidence, experience, preferences and decision processes despite having similar financial circumstances.

Revisit lesson 27: VALS profiles: Innovators & Survivors
Q054 · Lesson 27 · applicationReturn to question

A subscription team hypothesises that some cautious customers value transparent commitments, while more exploratory customers value demonstrations. What is the most appropriate next step?

D. Test the messages with actual customers and compare their responses

A Income alone does not establish caution or a validated profile. The team should investigate relevant motives and behaviour before assigning customers to groups or deciding how to communicate.

B Dated media descriptions are not dependable channel rules for current customers. Channel selection should use relevant audience evidence rather than infer habits from an unverified profile stereotype.

C The profiles suggest tendencies and hypotheses, not permanent rules about individuals. Preferences can vary with the offer and context, so actual customer responses should inform the decision.

D · correct Testing translates the framework into evidence about this audience and offer. Comparing responses helps the team refine its messages while avoiding unsupported judgements based on a profile label.

Revisit lesson 27: VALS profiles: Innovators & Survivors
Part 02 · Understand every option

Q055-Q057 · Reasoning

Q055 · Lesson 28 · foundationReturn to question

Which use of an Experiencer or Thinker profile provides the strongest basis for a communication decision?

A. Treat the profile as a hypothesis and test the message with customers.

A · correct Profiles suggest possible motivations, but customer evidence must establish whether a message works. Testing connects the framework to the actual audience and buying context.

B Age alone does not establish motivation or a validated profile. Customers of the same age can have different priorities, so this approach needs further evidence.

C A profile does not determine loyalty in every purchase. Behaviour can change with the category, circumstances and available alternatives, requiring investigation rather than automatic prediction.

D Emotional stories and rational evidence can reinforce each other. Excluding one automatically overlooks customers who want both an appealing experience and a credible practical justification.

Revisit lesson 28: VALS profiles: Experiencers & Thinkers
Q056 · Lesson 28 · applicationReturn to question

Research finds that prospective workshop customers compare practical outcomes, tutor experience and course structure before booking. Which communication should the provider test first?

C. A clear syllabus, tutor credentials and examples of completed practical work.

A Social scenes could communicate atmosphere, but they omit the comparison criteria identified in the research. This audience needs information that supports its practical evaluation of the course.

B A discount changes the financial offer but does not answer questions about outcomes or quality. Price incentives should not replace evidence addressing the stated decision criteria.

C · correct These materials directly address the observed evaluation process and provide reasons to believe the course promise. Their effect on understanding and bookings should still be measured.

D Celebrity recognition may attract attention, but lifestyle relevance does not establish tutor capability or course structure. The proposed message lacks evidence for the customers' stated concerns.

Revisit lesson 28: VALS profiles: Experiencers & Thinkers
Q057 · Lesson 29 · foundationReturn to question

A customer has a high monetary score in an RFM analysis. Which conclusion is justified by that score alone?

B. The customer spent relatively heavily within the defined scoring window.

A Spending is revenue evidence, not a complete profit measure. Discounts, returns, fulfilment and service costs can make a high-spending customer less profitable than the score suggests.

B · correct The monetary component records spending within a specified period and scoring convention. It supports a spending comparison, while profit, attitudes and usage require other evidence.

C RFM describes observed purchasing behaviour rather than emotional attachment. High spending could reflect convenience, limited alternatives or business requirements without demonstrating a strong preference for the brand.

D Purchase spending does not reveal consumption frequency directly. Customers might buy expensive items, purchase for others or hold inventory, so usage needs separate measurement or research.

Revisit lesson 29: Behavioural segmentation & RFM
Part 02 · Understand every option

Q058-Q060 · Reasoning

Q058 · Lesson 29 · applicationReturn to question

Today, Amal has been a customer for five years but last ordered 100 days ago. Dina joined ten days ago and ordered yesterday. Using time since latest purchase, which interpretation is correct?

D. Dina has stronger recency, while their frequency scores need more information.

A The length of the relationship measures tenure, not recency. Amal's last order was further in the past, regardless of how many years she has been a customer.

B Recency distinguishes customers by the elapsed time since their latest purchase. Having made any purchase establishes customer status but does not make their recency measures equal.

C The latest order establishes recency, but frequency requires an order count over a defined window. One recent purchase does not prove a higher frequency score.

D · correct Dina's purchase yesterday is more recent than Amal's purchase 100 days ago. Frequency cannot be ranked without the relevant order counts and a shared measurement period.

Revisit lesson 29: Behavioural segmentation & RFM
Q059 · Lesson 30 · foundationReturn to question

Why should a refrigerator retailer reconsider the RFM thresholds used by a weekly grocery service?

C. Normal purchase cycles change what recent and frequent behaviour means.

A Monetary value can still inform analysis of durable products. The issue is whether the measurement window and thresholds reflect the category, not whether spending becomes irrelevant.

B Scores should be consistently defined within an appropriate comparison group. They do not need to be identical across industries with different buying cycles and customer behaviour.

C · correct A long interval between refrigerator purchases may be normal, while the same interval could signal grocery inactivity. Thresholds need to reflect the expected category purchase cycle.

D Geography and behaviour answer different questions and can be combined. A long replacement cycle requires better behavioural definitions, not automatic removal of behavioural analysis altogether.

Revisit lesson 30: RFM scoring & geographic choices
Q060 · Lesson 30 · applicationReturn to question

R scores: 3 within 30 days, 2 at 31-90, 1 beyond 90. Six-month F scores: 3 for 6+ orders, 2 for 3-5, 1 below 3. M scores: 3 for EGP 1,200+, 2 for 600-1,199, 1 below 600. A customer last ordered 48 days ago, with seven orders totalling EGP 1,500. Which RFM code applies?

A. 233

A · correct Forty-eight days falls in the middle recency band, giving R2. Seven orders meet F3, and EGP 1,500 meets M3, producing the ordered code 233.

B This code incorrectly assigns the strongest recency band and the middle frequency band. The given thresholds assign R2 to 48 days and F3 to seven orders.

C The frequency and monetary digits are correct, but the recency digit is too high. A purchase 48 days ago falls outside the stated strongest recency band.

D The recency and frequency digits are correct, but the monetary digit is too low. Spending EGP 1,500 exceeds the stated EGP 1,200 threshold for M3.

Revisit lesson 30: RFM scoring & geographic choices

Q061-Q063 · Reasoning

Q061 · Lesson 31 · foundationReturn to question

Which observation adds a needs-based distinction to a B2B segment described by industry, size and location?

D. The organisation prioritises dependable support over the lowest purchase price.

A Employee count describes organisational size, a firmographic characteristic already represented in the segment. It does not explain which benefit or supplier response the organisation values most.

B Industry identifies the type of organisation and can help establish product relevance. It does not by itself distinguish the priorities that guide a particular buying decision.

C Branch locations add geographic detail that may affect delivery planning. They do not establish whether the buyer prioritises price, service, quality or a deeper supplier partnership.

D · correct The preference identifies the value sought in the supplier relationship. It can guide service design and communication alongside the organisation's firmographic and geographic characteristics.

Revisit lesson 31: Segmenting business customers
Q062 · Lesson 31 · applicationReturn to question

A warehouse is comparing equipment suppliers. Procurement stresses purchase price; users report that downtime disrupts orders. What should the supplier do to build a useful proposal?

B. Investigate both groups' criteria and show purchase, downtime and support costs.

A Procurement matters, but excluding users misses performance requirements that affect adoption and value. A proposal should recognise the buying group rather than assume one role represents everyone.

B · correct Combining buying-group insight with total-cost evidence addresses both commercial terms and operational impact. It supports a proposal based on value over use, rather than purchase price alone.

C A low purchase price may conceal costly downtime or support gaps. Making price the only promise ignores the operational need identified and may weaken the proposed value.

D Users provide essential insight but may not control terms, approvals or budgets. Treating them as the only decision makers risks overlooking procurement requirements within the buying process.

Revisit lesson 31: Segmenting business customers
Q063 · Lesson 32 · foundationReturn to question

A business creates separate offers for several customer groups with different needs. Which targeting approach best describes this choice?

A. Differentiated targeting.

A · correct Differentiated targeting serves multiple groups with tailored offers. The defining feature here is adapting the offer to several distinct needs, rather than using one broadly common offer.

B Undifferentiated targeting uses a broadly common offer when needs are sufficiently similar. Separate offers designed for different groups indicate a more tailored approach than this.

C Concentrated targeting focuses resources on a narrower selected group. The scenario instead describes serving several distinct groups with separate offers adapted to their different needs.

D Geographic segmentation divides a market using location-related factors. It is a segmentation basis, not the targeting approach described by choosing tailored offers for multiple groups.

Revisit lesson 32: Choose attractive, workable targets

Q064-Q066 · Reasoning

Q064 · Lesson 32 · applicationReturn to question

Segment A is larger than Segment B. Initial estimates show equal total contribution before acquisition costs. The firm can serve B well but needs expensive new infrastructure for A. What is the best next step?

C. Compare access costs, capability investment and risks before selecting the target.

A Size alone does not establish attractiveness or return. The equal contribution estimate and additional infrastructure requirement mean the larger segment could produce a weaker overall economic result.

B B appears promising because of organisational fit, but that is not a complete evaluation. Acquisition costs, access, competition and risk could still change the preferred choice.

C · correct The choice should combine segment attractiveness, organisational fit and full economics. Comparing the missing costs and risks allows the apparent contribution opportunity to be assessed realistically.

D Serving both groups would require resources and capabilities that have not been established. Differentiated targeting is a strategic option, not an automatic answer to incomplete segment analysis.

Revisit lesson 32: Choose attractive, workable targets
Q065 · Lesson 33 · foundationReturn to question

A positioning statement promises reliable delivery for small retailers. Which addition most directly strengthens its reason to believe?

B. Evidence of delivery performance and the capability supporting it.

A Expanding the claim to everyone weakens the clarity of the chosen target. It does not supply evidence that the business can deliver the promised reliability.

B · correct Credible performance evidence and an operational basis support the promised benefit. They help the target understand why it should believe the intended position relative to alternatives.

C A slogan may improve recognition, but an unrelated phrase does not substantiate reliability. Positioning needs a meaningful benefit and support that connects directly to the promise.

D Additional spending may distribute the claim more widely without making it more credible. Delivery evidence and capability are needed to support the promised customer experience.

Revisit lesson 33: Positioning: earn a place in the mind
Q066 · Lesson 33 · applicationReturn to question

A delivery service wants to be known as dependable. Research finds customers remember late arrivals and unclear tracking. Which action most directly supports the desired position?

D. Improve scheduling and tracking, then support the promise with verified performance.

A More repetition can increase exposure while leaving the causes of negative perceptions intact. A dependable position requires the service experience to support the communication consistently.

B Packaging may contribute physical evidence, but an unrelated improvement does not resolve late arrivals or unclear tracking. Resources should address the gaps undermining the specific promise.

C An internal preference exercise cannot replace evidence about customer perceptions or service capability. Changing words alone leaves the operational problems and their reputational effects unresolved.

D · correct The action connects the intended benefit to processes customers experience and evidence they can assess. It addresses the documented gap between the promise and current perceptions.

Revisit lesson 33: Positioning: earn a place in the mind

Q067-Q069 · Reasoning

Q067 · Lesson 34 · foundationReturn to question

A furniture factory buys timber incorporated into tables and printer paper used in its accounts office. How should these purchases be classified?

C. Timber is a raw material; printer paper is an operating supply.

A An installation is a major capital item, while accessory equipment assists operations. Neither classification fits consumable timber entering production or paper supporting office work in this scenario.

B Being purchased by a factory does not make an item a product component. Classification depends on its role in production or operations, not simply the purchaser.

C · correct The timber becomes part of the manufactured product, making it a raw material. The accounts-office paper supports operations without entering the furniture sold to customers.

D These roles are reversed. Timber enters the tables being manufactured, whereas printer paper supports office activity and does not become a material in the finished furniture.

Revisit lesson 34: The 7Ps & business products
Q068 · Lesson 34 · applicationReturn to question

A training company promises a premium learning experience but has confusing booking, unprepared staff and unreliable rooms. Which response best applies the 7Ps?

A. Align staff preparation, booking processes and learning surroundings with the promise.

A · correct People, process and physical evidence directly shape the reported experience. Improving them makes the marketing mix more coherent with the premium position communicated to learners.

B Price can signal positioning, but a higher price does not correct poor delivery. It could increase expectations while the same booking, staffing and facility problems remain.

C Promotion communicates a promise that the current experience fails to support. Increasing exposure without addressing delivery could widen the gap between expectations and customer experience.

D Course content is part of the offer, but additional topics do not resolve the specified service weaknesses. The mix needs coordinated improvements across the relevant elements.

Revisit lesson 34: The 7Ps & business products
Q069 · Lesson 35 · foundationReturn to question

A buyer travels to a distant store for one particular camera and refuses substitutes. Which consumer product classification best fits this buying behaviour?

D. Speciality, because a specific preference motivates extra purchasing effort.

A A completed brand choice does not make a purchase convenient in the classification sense. The deliberate extra effort and refusal of substitutes indicate a strong specific preference.

B Shopping behaviour typically involves comparing alternatives, but the scenario emphasises commitment to one model. Product classifications depend on the buyer's behaviour, not an automatic category rule.

C Unsought products are not actively sought or considered. This buyer is deliberately seeking a specific camera, so inconvenience or travel distance does not establish unsought behaviour.

D · correct The buyer has a particular preference strong enough to justify extra effort and reject alternatives. That behaviour fits a speciality purchase in this specific buying situation.

Revisit lesson 35: Product types & three levels of value
